report:
## Conclusion: Yes — but specifically for the most severely ill patients

The evidence strongly supports that dexamethasone (and similar corticosteroids) improves survival in critically ill, hospitalized COVID-19 patients — but the benefit is limited to those requiring supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation, not mild cases.

**Key evidence:**

1. **RECOVERY Trial (Oxford University, UK)** — a large randomized controlled trial of over 6,000 hospitalized patients — found dexamethasone reduced 28-day mortality by about one-third in patients on invasive mechanical ventilation, and by about one-fifth in patients receiving oxygen alone. No mortality benefit was seen in patients not requiring oxygen support. The trial estimated that treating roughly 8 ventilated patients, or 25 patients on oxygen, would prevent one death (https://www.recoverytrial.net/news/low-cost-dexamethasone-reduces-death-by-up-to-one-third-in-hospitalised-patients-with-severe-respiratory-complications-of-covid-19). The full peer-reviewed results were published in the New England Journal of Medicine (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436).

2. **WHO-sponsored prospective meta-analysis (JAMA, 2020)** — pooling data from seven randomized trials of systemic corticosteroids in critically ill COVID-19 patients — found corticosteroid treatment was associated with lower 28-day all-cause mortality compared with usual care or placebo, reinforcing the RECOVERY findings across multiple trials and steroid types (hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, methylprednisolone) (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2770279).

3. Coverage from the BBC summarized the clinical and public-health significance: dexamethasone became the first drug shown to reduce mortality in COVID-19, is cheap and globally available (https://www.bbc.com/news/health-53077879).

**Caveat:** The benefit is specific to hypoxic, hospitalized patients; steroids showed no benefit — and some signal of possible harm — in patients not needing oxygen, so timing and severity matter.
